newsitem.title: USA: Researchers say new prostate test avoids many biopsies.
newsitem.headline: Researchers say new prostate test avoids many biopsies.

text.p: A new version of a common screening test can detect 95 percent of prostate cancers while avoiding many needless biopsies, researchers said on Sunday.

Lead researcher Dr. William J. Catalona, professor of surgery and head of the Division of Urologic Surgery at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, said the test works well regardless of a man's age or the size of his prostate.
"Now we can detect cancer early, and perhaps save lives, without so many false alarms," he said. The research was presented at the American Urological Association meeting.

Catalona said the study involved 773 men who, through the traditional prostate cancer screening test, had total prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels between four and 10, a gray zone where doctors usually can't confirm or rule out prostate cancer without a biopsy.
Doctors conducted the new test, which measures the percentage of PSA that floats freely in the blood, or free PSA, and then performed biopsies on all of the patients.
The free PSA test will be reviewed soon by the Federal Drug Administration, he said. The study, because of its size, was expected to speed FDA approval, he said.

Ninety-five percent of the men diagnosed with cancer had free PSA levels of less than 25 percent, he said. Based on those results, doctors should recommend biopsies for all men with free PSA levels below 25 percent.

Previous studies indicated a low percentage of free PSA is a strong signal for prostate cancer, but doctors did not have a tool to determine what percentage was the best cutoff point for biopsies. If it were set too low, many cancers would go undetected. Also the patient's age is a factor in the possibility of cancer, as is the prostate size.

"We wanted to avoid using many different cutoffs ... something that was practical and easy to remember," Catalona said. A cutoff of 25 percent worked well for the study group as a whole, he said. The single standard would have caught 98 percent of cancers for men in their 50s and 90 percent for those in their early 70s.
He said the cancers that did not meet the cutoff tended to be less aggressive.
